tagline.text: Philosophy that starts from the single person who must choose how to live.

overview.text: Existentialism is a loose family of ideas, not a tidy school. It starts from life as a person lives it, not from a detached viewpoint. Its central idea is that we are not born with a fixed nature. We make ourselves through our choices, and we are responsible for who we become. Two nineteenth-century thinkers laid the groundwork: Kierkegaard, from Denmark, and Nietzsche, a German philosopher. In mid-twentieth-century France, Sartre and Beauvoir made it famous.

sources.quote: certainly not a reference to a coherent system or philosophical school
the most popular voices of this movement were French
He spent most of his life in and around the Danish capital

overview.text: It rejects fixed moral rules, but it does not say that morality is empty. A good life is possible: one where we own our choices and help others be free too. Above all, it takes on questions we all meet:
items: How do I live when no rulebook tells me how?
How do I stop drifting along with the crowd?
How do I face anxiety, death and a sense that life is meaningless?

questions.text: If nothing hands me a purpose, how do I live?

themes.title: Existence before essence
themes.summary: We are not born with a fixed nature. We make ourselves through what we choose.

paragraphs.text: Sartre called it 'the first principle of existentialism': existence precedes essence. Your 'essence' would be a fixed nature that decides who you are. Existentialists say there is none. A person first 'turns up' and only afterwards defines himself, through choices made as life unfolds. Sartre adapted the idea from Heidegger, a German philosopher. Hard facts still limit us, such as our body and the time and place we live in. Existentialists call these facts our 'facticity'. But we can question them, give them meaning and decide what to do with them. This power to rise above the facts is called 'transcendence'.

sources.quote: the first principle of existentialism
not as a substance or thing with some pre-given nature
twentieth-century German philosophers like Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger, and Karl Jaspers

themes.title: Freedom and anxiety
themes.summary: Being free means I alone answer for my choices, and that feels dizzying.

paragraphs.text: If nothing fixed decides who we are, then we are free. We are also responsible for what we make of ourselves. Take Sartre's example of a coward. Childhood or genes did not make him that way; he 'makes himself a coward' by his decisions. Seeing this brings anxiety. No god and no absolute moral rule can choose for us or excuse us. In Sartre's words, there are 'no excuses behind us nor justifications before us'. Kierkegaard called anxiety 'the dizziness of freedom'. Existentialists ask us to face this feeling, not run from it. It can shake us out of our comfortable routines.

sources.quote: there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us

sources.section: 2. Kierkegaard’s Analysis of Human Existence: Despair, Social Critique, and Anxiety
sources.quote: anxiety is the dizziness of freedom

themes.title: Authenticity versus the crowd
themes.summary: Most of the time we just do what everyone else does. Being authentic means living our own life.

paragraphs.text: Being authentic means being true to yourself. Existentialists criticise living by rules and expectations we pick up from others. As Heidegger put it, we enjoy, read and judge things as 'they' do. Doing what everyone does is comforting, because it feels like living well. But it hides our freedom from us. Sartre and Beauvoir call this self-deception 'bad faith'. I am in bad faith when I treat myself as a fixed thing: 'I am what I am'. I am also in bad faith when I pretend my situation puts no limits on my choices. Several thinkers had a name for the crowd we drift with:

sources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity

sources.quote: prevents us from being authentic or true to ourselves

items: Kierkegaard: 'the public'
Nietzsche: 'the herd'
Heidegger: 'the They'

paragraphs.text: What authenticity looks like varies by thinker:
items: Kierkegaard: a passionate commitment that pulls a scattered life together.
Nietzsche: saying yes to your whole life, even to living it again forever.
Heidegger: 'resoluteness', a focused grip on your chosen path that stays open to letting it go.
Sartre and Beauvoir: seeing your unsettled situation clearly, accepting it, and taking responsibility for what you do.

themes.title: Meaning without guarantees
themes.summary: Without God or a built-in purpose, meaning has to be made, not found.

paragraphs.text: As nineteenth-century Europe became less religious and more scientific, the old religious picture that gave life moral direction began to collapse. Nietzsche diagnosed the result: nihilism, the shocking sense that our existence has no overall reason or purpose. His image for this loss was 'the death of God'. The French novelist Albert Camus called our situation 'the absurd'. It is the clash between our 'wild longing for clarity' and 'the unreasonable silence of the world'. Yet this need not end in despair. For Camus, the absurd calls for action, not suicide. Beauvoir held that existence is not absurd but ambiguous: its meaning is never fixed, so we keep making it.

themes.title: My freedom needs yours
themes.summary: Other people can trap us as objects, yet my freedom depends on theirs.

paragraphs.text: Sartre and Beauvoir argued that we see ourselves through 'the look' of others. Their gaze can turn us into objects. Relationships then become a power struggle. Sartre's play No Exit sums this up in its famous line that hell is other people. But there is a better way. Beauvoir's 'authentic love' nurtures the other person's freedom instead of possessing them. She and Sartre concluded that wanting my own freedom commits me to wanting it for others. In Beauvoir's words, to will oneself free is also to will others free. Later, Sartre shifted his focus from the single person to society. Three things pushed him:

sources.quote: Hell is—other people

themes.title: Faith and the leap
themes.summary: For religious existentialists, faith is a personal commitment reason can't justify.

paragraphs.text: Existentialism is not only atheist. Kierkegaard was a Christian. He prized 'a truth which is true for me', lived and felt rather than proved. His book Fear and Trembling retells the Bible story in which God tells Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. Abraham becomes a 'knight of faith': someone who commits to a truth that reason cannot make sense of. He 'leaps' into a paradox, alone with a choice no one else understands. The Jewish thinker Martin Buber stressed meeting another person as a 'You', a whole person. The opposite is treating them as an 'It', a thing to use. Nietzsche and Sartre, by contrast, saw God as irrelevant or even harmful to our deepest choices.

sources.quote: a truth which is true for me

paragraphs.text: Early hints of this outlook go back to ancient philosophy and to later writers on death and the meaning of life. But the ideas became a movement only in the nineteenth century. Religion's hold was fading, and industry and bureaucracy made society feel impersonal. Early voices included:

paragraphs.text: In the twentieth century, German thinkers such as Husserl, Jaspers and Heidegger laid more groundwork. They gave the movement its roots in phenomenology: the study of how we experience the world from our own point of view. Heidegger's book Being and Time (1927) shaped Sartre and Beauvoir. The movement then exploded in France in the middle of the century. Sartre's Being and Nothingness appeared in 1943, the year the French thinker Gabriel Marcel coined the word 'existentialism'. Its backdrop was:

sources.quote: Existentialism’s phenomenological roots
the study of how an individual encounters the world through first-person experience

items: the Second World War

the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

paragraphs.text: Who counts as an existentialist is disputed. The word names no single set of beliefs. Most thinkers grouped under it never used it, or rejected it. Only Sartre and Beauvoir openly claimed it. In 1947 Heidegger rejected any link between his thought and Sartre's existentialism. Yet both encyclopedias we draw on, Stanford's and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, still count him as a key figure. Camus gave a 1945 interview titled, in English, 'No, I am not an existentialist'. Even so, the Stanford encyclopedia places his essay The Myth of Sisyphus squarely in the tradition.

paragraphs.text: In Germany, critics such as Adorno called existentialism obscure, abstract and even mystical, Heidegger above all. Many other philosophers agreed. After Marxist criticism in the 1940s and 1950s, Sartre himself decided his early idea of 'radical' freedom, made by choice alone, was too abstract. It ignored the social conditions that limit real choices. The French philosopher Merleau-Ponty objected that no one is free apart from other people and history. Later French thinkers faulted Sartre for neglecting language and the impersonal structures that shape meaning.

sources.section: e. Simone de Beauvoir (1908-1986) as an Existentialist Philosopher

sources.quote: French thinker Maurice Merleau-Ponty

paragraphs.text: Other criticisms are moral and political. Critics said existentialists neglected social and political structures, with dangerous results. Heidegger is notorious for his involvement with the Nazis in the 1930s. Nietzsche's ideal of the self-creating individual is openly elitist and anti-democratic. The Nazis exploited his work, a use the Internet Encyclopedia calls 'utterly misdirected'. Camus accused Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Heidegger of escaping into 'forced hope'. He meant turning to God, or something beyond this life, to escape the absurd. Some argue the label does more harm than good, lumping very different ideas together.

paragraphs.text: Among philosophers, verdicts differ. The Internet Encyclopedia finds the movement as a whole has had relatively little direct influence there. Yet Nietzsche and Heidegger remain very much alive. It adds that the movement made emotion a serious subject of research. The movement also insisted that philosophy deal directly with real-life topics such as sex and death. The Stanford encyclopedia sees the movement thriving, and its courses are among philosophy's most popular. In its view, the movement has shaped:

thinkers.name: Søren Kierkegaard
thinkers.summary: Søren Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813 and wrote mostly in the 1840s, across philosophy, theology, psychology and social critique. He opposed building grand systems and is often called the 'father of existentialism', though SEP warns the label hides as much as it shows. He has often been cast as Hegel's great opponent, but recent scholars think his main target was certain Danish Hegelians.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher and cultural critic who published intensively in the 1870s and 1880s. He is famous for fierce attacks on traditional European morality and religion, often by exposing the hidden psychology behind received ideas. He also proposed new values he hoped would renew culture, and SEP's existentialism entry counts him among the movement's nineteenth-century pioneers.

key_ideas.text: 'God is dead': belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable, so the morality built on it is set to collapse.
Imagine living your life over and over forever; on one influential reading, your reaction tests how much you value your life (eternal recurrence).

thinkers.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
thinkers.summary: Jean-Paul Sartre was, with Simone de Beauvoir, the most popular voice of mid-twentieth-century French existentialism, and a novelist, playwright and public intellectual. His treatise Being and Nothingness (1943) is called the defining work of the movement, and his 1945 lecture Existentialism is a Humanism drew huge crowds. Later he tried to combine existentialism with Marxism.

key_ideas.text: Existence precedes essence: we turn up first and define ourselves afterward through our choices.
We are 'condemned' to be free: no fact about our situation fixes how we respond to it, so we are responsible.
Bad faith is self-deception: denying either our freedom or the facts of our situation.

thinkers.name: Simone de Beauvoir
thinkers.summary: Simone de Beauvoir was a philosopher, novelist, feminist and activist, and one of the major figures of post-war French existentialism. She is best known for The Second Sex (1949), her trailblazing work in feminist philosophy. She called herself an author rather than a philosopher, but scholarship has secured her place as a thinker in her own right, not merely Sartre's helper.

thinkers.name: Albert Camus
thinkers.summary: Albert Camus was a journalist, novelist, playwright and essayist who more than once denied being a philosopher. His Myth of Sisyphus sits squarely in the existentialist tradition, yet he denied being an existentialist and wrote against Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Heidegger. He won the Nobel Prize for literature in 1957 and died in a car accident in 1960.

intro.text: Existentialists do not look at life from a cool distance. They start from a person caught up in living. Kierkegaard wanted 'a truth which is true for me', lived and felt rather than just known. Their ideas also shaped existential psychotherapy, which helps people with questions such as meaning and the fear of death. One example is logotherapy, a therapy built around finding meaning, invented by the Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl.

idea.text: For existentialists, no god and no absolute moral law can guide our choices or justify them. We alone are responsible, and realising that often brings anxiety. As Sartre put it, 'there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us'.

practice.text: Sartre's own example is a student of his in wartime France. The student's brother had been killed in the German attack of 1940. He could go to England and fight with the Free French Forces. Or he could stay with his mother, who lived only for him. He came to Sartre for advice. But choosing an adviser, Sartre said, is already a choice: you more or less know what they will say. His only reply was 'You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent.' One way to use his point: before your next hard choice, ask yourself why you picked the person you are asking, and what you already expect them to say.

sources.quote: to choose an adviser is nevertheless to commit oneself by that choice
You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent
the choice between going to England to join the Free French Forces or of staying near his mother

idea.text: For Sartre and Beauvoir, no fixed meaning is handed to us. Beauvoir said existence is not absurd but ambiguous: 'its meaning is never fixed'. A 2015 review pooled the results of 15 trials of existential therapies. Meaning-focused therapies had large effects on people's sense of meaning. It found most support for structured programmes that discussed meaning directly with physically ill patients. But the studies were few and low in quality. That is evidence for therapy, not for reflecting alone.

practice.text: Frankl held that we discover meaning rather than make it. He turned the usual question round: we should not ask what life means, but recognise 'that it is he who is asked'. In therapy, logotherapists often use Socratic dialogue: guiding a person by asking questions. They help clients find meanings for themselves. The Viktor Frankl Institute of Logotherapy names three avenues to meaning. One way to borrow that on your own: this week, ask yourself how each avenue showed up for you.

idea.text: For Nietzsche, the key to giving your life its own style is radical acceptance. That means saying yes to your whole life, the good and the bad. He called this attitude amor fati: love of one's fate. He also thought only 'the highest types' have that kind of freedom.

practice.text: Imagine a demon tells you that you must live this life again, 'innumerable times', with nothing new in it. Would you curse the demon? Or would you answer that you never heard anything more divine? If the thought took hold of you, Nietzsche wrote, it would transform you, or perhaps crush you. The question 'Dost thou want this once more, and also for innumerable times?' would lie as the heaviest burden on everything you do. One influential reading treats it as a test of whether your life has been good. He meant your life as a whole, in every detail. If that feels too big, one way in (our adaptation, not his): ask it of a single day first.

sources.quote: If that thought acquired power over thee, as thou art, it would transform thee, and perhaps crush thee
